title: Aerobic versus anaerobic activity
summary: Sustained aerobic movement and short bursts of intense effort use energy differently.
why: The glucose direction in a gentle walk may differ from that during a sprint.
how: Working muscles take up glucose. Intense effort can also trigger liver glucose release through stress hormones.
example: A learner compares a steady jog with a short hill sprint at the same time of day.
caution: Exercise responses vary with insulin on board, fuel and fitness. The activity name is never a dosing rule.
question: Can glucose rise during exercise?
answer: Yes, particularly during intense or competitive effort.
takeaways: Consider effort as well as duration

title: Walking, running, cycling and swimming
summary: These activities can involve sustained use of large muscles, with very different intensity and access to supplies.
why: Swimming and cycling can make it harder to stop and check a reading quickly.
how: Glucose use depends on pace, duration and recent insulin. Water may interrupt device communication.
example: A swimmer arranges poolside access to a meter and low treatment before entering the water.
caution: Check device water ratings and use your own safety plan. Do not rely on a distant phone alarm underwater.
question: Is every walk a low-intensity session?
answer: Terrain, pace and fitness can substantially alter effort.

title: Strength training
summary: Resistance exercise uses muscles against a load, often in short sets with rest periods.
why: The glucose curve during lifting can differ from the hours after training.
how: Short intense sets may raise glucose temporarily while recovering muscles later take up glucose.
example: Someone records sets and rest times alongside their reading after a gym session.
caution: Avoid reacting to a brief rise with unplanned corrections. Discuss repeated patterns.
question: Can a strength session still be followed by a low?
answer: Yes. Later sensitivity can increase even after a stable or rising session.

title: High-intensity exercise
summary: Hard intervals and competition can briefly raise glucose despite high energy use.
why: A post-session high does not necessarily mean there was too little insulin throughout the activity.
how: Adrenaline helps mobilise glucose faster than muscles take it up during some intense efforts.
example: A footballer compares a competitive match with a relaxed practice session.
caution: Illness or ketones are different from an exercise-related rise. Follow the ketone and activity plan if unwell.
question: Should everyone expect a spike after intervals?
answer: No. Starting glucose, insulin, food and intensity all matter.
takeaways: A temporary rise has several causes

title: Delayed hypoglycemia after activity
summary: A low may occur hours after an activity has finished.
why: Feeling well immediately after a session does not remove the later risk.
how: Recovering muscles replenish stored fuel, and insulin sensitivity can remain higher.
example: A learner notes a late-afternoon low following a longer-than-usual morning walk.
caution: Discuss recurring delayed lows and the follow-up monitoring window with the team.
question: Is finishing exercise the end of glucose monitoring?

title: Nighttime lows after exercise
summary: Late-day activity may affect glucose during sleep.
why: A sleeping person may miss the usual early warnings.
how: Greater sensitivity and muscle recovery can continue overnight. Basal insulin remains active during sleep.
example: After evening badminton a family follows their agreed overnight monitoring plan.
caution: Review frequent overnight alarms or lows with the team. Do not assume every low trace is an artefact.
question: What should I record for a review?
answer: Activity timing, intensity, meals, insulin and the overnight trace.

title: Exercise and insulin sensitivity
summary: Insulin sensitivity describes how strongly tissues respond to available insulin.
why: After some activities, usual routines can produce different glucose responses.
how: Muscle contraction and insulin both promote glucose uptake. Training and recovery can change that balance over time.
example: A person compares the day after a hike with a typical office day.
caution: Changes are individual. Avoid copying someone else’s percentage adjustment.
question: Does improved sensitivity have a fixed duration?
answer: No. Duration depends on the session and the person.

title: Reading a CGM during activity
summary: A CGM shows a trend during movement, with limits when glucose is changing quickly.
why: A falling arrow during exercise can matter even before an alarm sounds.
how: Interstitial readings can lag blood glucose. Water, pressure or lost signal may affect what reaches the display.
example: A runner with symptoms inconsistent with the sensor stops safely and follows the meter-confirmation plan.
caution: Keep backup monitoring accessible. A trend arrow is not a guaranteed forecast.
question: Can I rely on the last number during signal loss?
answer: An old number may not describe current glucose. Follow the backup plan.

title: Trekking and endurance
summary: Long activities add challenges of distance, variable pace and delayed access to food or help.
why: A supply that is enough for a usual gym session may be insufficient on a remote trail.
how: Heat, altitude, effort and changing meal times can affect monitoring, insulin storage and glucose response.
example: A trekking group identifies rest points, a turnaround plan and the person carrying spare supplies.
caution: Plan remote trips with the care team. Keep rescue carbohydrate within reach rather than in checked or distant luggage.
question: What can a companion help with?
answer: Knowing where supplies are, how to recognise trouble and how to summon help.

title: Sports safety preparation
summary: A sports plan brings monitoring, low treatment, hydration and emergency contacts together.
why: A written plan makes it easier to respond when a game or event becomes hectic.
how: Discuss starting conditions, symptoms, ketones, equipment and when to pause with the team.
example: A coach learns where the athlete keeps rescue supplies and who to call if they cannot self-treat.
caution: Do not begin or continue activity through suspected ketoacidosis or a severe low.
question: What is worth practising before competition?
answer: Stopping safely, accessing monitoring and getting help from a teammate.
